note: Posts from TDI-owned voice accounts. Comments describe the tool, what to change, or who it suits. None claims a classroom moment and none cites an internal number.

posts: Four covers most weeks. The concern email is the one worth reading twice before you adapt it, because tone carries further in writing than people expect.
Keep the positive one ready to send rather than saved for a reason. It is the one that gets used least and earns most.
Which of the four do you reach for most, and which have you never needed?
How do you adjust these for a family you have not met yet?
Judgment-free is the design requirement. Any homework advice that implies the family is doing it wrong stops being read at the second line.
Send two or three, not the whole set. A list of strategies reads as a list of expectations.
What do families most often ask you about homework?
What do you say to a parent who is doing the homework themselves?
Plain language is the whole job here. Families do not need to know how the tools work, they need to know what is allowed and what happens if it is not.
Send it before an incident, not in response to one. The same letter reads completely differently in each case.
What have families asked you about AI that you were not ready for?
Does your policy differ from the building's, and does the letter say so?
Prepare your questions as carefully as your talking points. A conference where only the teacher asks anything is a report, not a meeting.
Bring one piece of data, not four. The second and third get argued about and the first gets remembered.
What question do you ask families that opens the conversation up?
How long are your conference slots, and is that long enough to be honest in?
The point is to know your first two sentences and your last one. The middle mostly takes care of itself.
Check what time is actually reachable for the family before you call. Three missed calls reads as avoidance in both directions.
What time of day do you make hard calls, and why that time?
Do you prepare differently for a meeting you called versus one the family asked for?
Lead with the problem in your building rather than the product. An administrator hears a pitch as another initiative unless it is attached to something they already worry about.
The funding section is the part most people skip and the part that decides whether the conversation continues.
What does your administrator actually need to hear before they will look at anything new?
Who makes this kind of decision in your building, and is it who you would expect?
Tone is the section worth rereading. Clarity is easy to fix later and tone is not.
Write the hard email, then leave it unsent overnight. Nothing in here beats that.
What is your rule for when an email should have been a conversation?
Have you ever sent one you wish you had not? What would have stopped you?
Starter is accurate. Circles run badly do more damage than not running them, and the guide is honest about the preparation involved.
Do not run your first circle about the worst thing that has happened. Practice on something small and boring first.
Has a circle ever gone wrong for you? What went wrong?
What do you do when a student refuses to take part?
The formula exists because feedback in a specialist setting has to be usable by a student who may not read tone. Specific and warm are not in tension here.
Works for support staff giving feedback too, which matters when the para is the one with the student most of the day.
How do you give corrective feedback without it landing as failure?
Who gives feedback in your setting, and is anyone coached on how?
Set the expectations before the visit, in writing. Almost every observation that goes badly does so because nobody agreed what it was for.
Give the parent something to look for. An observer with no task watches their own child and nothing else.
How often do parents observe where you are, and who arranges it?
What would you want said to your class before a parent walked in?
Pairing speech with visuals is the single change with the widest effect here, and it costs nothing.
The AAC section deserves care. A device that is not within reach is not available, whatever the plan says.
What have you changed about how you speak that made the most difference?
How do you make sure everyone who works with the student is doing the same thing?
Role clarity is the part that actually changes days. Most teacher and para friction is about unclear roles rather than unwillingness.
Use the planning templates together, once, at the start. Filled in separately they describe two different jobs.
For teachers, do you know what your para thinks their role is?
For paras, what would you change about how the day is planned if you were asked?
Daily and small is the design. A relationship strategy that needs a spare twenty minutes will not survive a normal week.
Track which students you have not spoken to individually. That is the list this is really for.
Which student in your room have you spoken to least this week?
What is your smallest habit that students seem to notice most?
Being open to feedback and being good at giving it are different skills, and most people score very differently on the two halves.
Answer about the last piece of feedback you actually received rather than in general. The general answer is always kinder.
When did you last change something because a colleague told you to?
For leaders, how do you know whether your staff feel able to give you feedback?
Precise rather than scripted. The difference matters, because reciting a line you do not mean is worse than the clumsy sentence you would have said.
Pick two or three and use them until they are yours. Trying to use all of it makes you sound like somebody else.
What is a phrase you use constantly that works, and where did you get it?
Which situation in here do you still not have good words for?
Three audiences, and the colleague scripts are the hardest to use because you have to keep working with them afterwards.
Firm is not the same as final. The scripts leave the door open on purpose.
Whose pushback do you find hardest, students, families or colleagues?
What do you say when you are being pushed on something you privately agree with?
Sentence starters are scaffolding, which means they are meant to come away. Worth planning when that happens rather than leaving them up all year.
The peer feedback starters are the most useful set here, because that is the one students have least language for.
At what point do you take the starters away, and how do you know?
Which starter do your students use most, and does it show up in their writing too?
Beyond pizza is the right framing. Food is easy to arrange and easy to read as the least anyone could do.
Specific beats generous. Being named for a particular thing lands harder than a gift card that went to everyone.
What recognition have you received that actually meant something?
What gets celebrated in your building, and what gets missed entirely?
Intentional is the operative word. Most teacher and para partnerships are assembled out of whatever the timetable did, and this is an attempt to choose instead.
Revisit it in November. The roles agreed in August rarely describe what is actually happening by then.
How much planning time do you get together, honestly?
What is the thing you have never managed to say to your teaching partner?
Built for hybrid as much as fully remote, which is the harder case because half the room is present and half is not.
Cameras off is not disengagement. The card assumes that, and it is worth assuming.
What actually works to reach a student you only ever see on a screen?
How do you run a discussion where some students are in the room and some are not?
Weekly rather than daily, because the point is to catch what slipped rather than to add another daily task.
Do it on the same day every week. Friday is the obvious choice and the worst one, because Friday is when nothing gets done.
Which of the three, families, team or admin, slips first for you?
What day do you do yours, and did you arrive at that deliberately?
Weekly or monthly is a real choice, not a preference. Monthly and actually sent beats weekly and abandoned in October.
Lead with what is coming rather than what happened. Families act on the first and skim the second.
Do families read yours? Have you ever found out?
What do you include that takes the least time and gets the most response?
The four types are about hard conversations specifically, not conversation generally. People often score as something they would not recognise socially.
The useful move afterwards is to borrow from the style you scored lowest on, in one specific situation, and see what happens.
Which of the four did you come out as, and did it feel fair?
Which style do you find hardest to be on the receiving end of?
